guide.title: Koreatown, Manhattan: Thirty-Two Blocks Called Korea Way
guide.intro: Koreatown emerged in the 1980s, when a Korean bookstore and a handful of Korean restaurants opened on what had been part of the Garment District; their success, aided by tourist traffic from the nearby Empire State Building and Macy's Herald Square, drew more Korean-owned businesses. The neighborhood's heart is Korea Way — West 32nd Street between Fifth and Sixth Avenues — known for its vertical, Seoul-like commerce, with restaurants, karaoke bars, and salons stacked on multiple floors of the same buildings, some running 24/7 to keep up with rents and foot traffic. Manhattan's Korean population nearly doubled between 2000 and 2010, to roughly 20,000 residents, part of a New York metro Korean population of 218,764 — the second-largest concentration of ethnic Koreans outside Korea — and since around 2015 the neighborhood has been expanding eastward toward Madison Avenue into Murray Hill, Kips Bay, and Rose Hill. Koreatown has also held an annual Korean Pride Festival each October since 2022.

sections.heading: A Newspaper Rivalry, Then Korea Way
sections.body: The neighborhood's Wikipedia profile describes it as home to over 150 businesses of various types and sizes, while the NYC Korean Chamber of Commerce estimates more than 100 small businesses on Korea Way itself. At the neighborhood's northwest corner, Greeley Square is named for New York Tribune publisher Horace Greeley, a rival of the New York Herald that named adjacent Herald Square; an 1890 bronze statue of Greeley by Alexander Doyle stands in the square, which the 34th Street Partnership business-improvement district has maintained since 1992, restoring its public restrooms in 2020.

sections.heading: Getting there by subway
sections.body: Koreatown sits one block from 34th Street–Herald Square (B/D/F/M and N/Q/R/W), with an out-of-system transfer to PATH's 33rd Street station. The 1/2/3 and A/C/E at 34th Street–Penn Station are about a 5-minute walk west, so nearly every trunk line lands within a couple of blocks of Korea Way.

faq.question: How do I get to Koreatown by subway?
faq.answer: 34th Street–Herald Square (B/D/F/M, N/Q/R/W) is one block away, with an out-of-system PATH transfer at 33rd Street. The 1/2/3 and A/C/E at 34th Street–Penn Station are about a 5-minute walk west.

faq.question: Why is it called Korea Way?
faq.answer: West 32nd Street between Fifth and Sixth Avenues became the commercial spine of Koreatown after Korean-owned businesses took root here in the 1980s, drawing on tourist traffic from the Empire State Building and Macy's Herald Square nearby.

faq.question: What is Greeley Square named for?
faq.answer: New York Tribune publisher Horace Greeley — a rival of James Gordon Bennett's New York Herald, for which neighboring Herald Square is named. An 1890 bronze statue of Greeley by Alexander Doyle stands in the square.

faq.question: Where can I stay in Koreatown?
faq.answer: Hotel Stanford, at 43 W 32nd Street, sits directly on Korea Way with major Midtown landmarks within walking distance.

faq.question: Can you still go up the Empire State Building from here?
faq.answer: Yes — the observatory at 20 West 34th Street borders Koreatown, with 86th- and 102nd-floor decks open 365 days a year, 9 a.m. to midnight.

places.name: Empire State Building Observatory
places.summary: The 1931 Art Deco skyscraper's 86th- and 102nd-floor observatories offer 360-degree views spanning up to six states. Open 365 days a year, 9 a.m. to midnight, with Main Deck tickets from $44 plus a booking fee.

places.name: Greeley Square Park
places.address: Triangle bounded by W 32nd and 33rd Streets, Broadway and Sixth Avenue, New York, NY
places.summary: A triangle plaza named for New York Tribune publisher Horace Greeley, whose 1890 bronze statue by Alexander Doyle stands here; maintained since 1992 by the 34th Street Partnership, with bistro seating and public restrooms restored in 2020.

places.name: Korean Cultural Center New York
places.summary: A government cultural institute under Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, offering free gallery exhibitions, film screenings, and performing-arts programs. Open Monday–Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

places.name: Cho Dang Gol
places.summary: A tofu house specializing in homemade tofu made fresh every morning, alongside traditional Korean dishes; walk-ins only.

places.name: New Wonjo
places.summary: A Korean BBQ restaurant on Korea Way open nearly around the clock, daily 10 a.m. to 5 a.m. with the kitchen open until 4 a.m.; the restaurant's own site dates it to 1993.

places.name: Osamil
places.summary: A modern Korean gastropub on Koreatown's southern edge with daily specials, weekend brunch, and late hours until 1 a.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.

places.name: HanGawi
places.summary: A long-running plant-based Korean restaurant known for its serene shoes-off dining room and vegetarian temple-style cuisine.

places.name: Hotel Stanford
places.summary: A long-standing hotel directly on Korea Way, with major Midtown landmarks within walking distance; rooms have smart TVs, climate control, and blackout curtains.
